performers: Louis Krasner, violin; The Cleveland Orchestra; Artur Rodzinski
intro: The first movement of Berg’s Violin Concerto is an Andante, which Berg thought of as a Praeludium, followed by an Allegretto that quotes a Carinthian folk song. Louis Krasner plays it with the Cleveland Orchestra under Artur Rodzinski, in a recording made on 15 December 1940.

sections.label: A · Andante: preluding on the open strings

cues.title: Opening: harp, clarinets, open strings
cues.text: The concerto begins in utmost quiet, with harp and clarinets preluding. The solo violin enters by touching its four open strings, from G up to E and down again. A clear cadence follows, and the first movement proper begins over a simple accompanying figure.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the music “starts in utmost quiet as harp and clarinets with solo violin begin some exploratory preluding”; the violin’s entrance is a touching of the four open strings from G up to E and down again, followed by a clear cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Krasner at the Wörthersee
cues.text: In June 1935 Krasner spent some time with Berg at his country house on the Wörthersee and improvised for hours, so that Berg could learn his playing. On 16 July Berg wrote to him that he had finished the composition the day before.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: Krasner’s visit in June, his improvising “so that Berg might get to know the strengths and characteristics of his technique”, and Berg’s letter of 16 July.

cues.title: The twelve-note row enters
cues.text: The violin’s next entrance again begins on the open G string and rises through the twelve-note row: G, B♭, D, F♯, A, C, E, G♯, B, C♯, E♭, F. Four triads within the row begin on the violin’s four open strings.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: “When the violin next enters, it again begins on the open G string”, with the pitches G B♭ D F♯ A C E G♯ B C♯ E♭ F; the open-string notes are the roots of the row’s four triads. Douglas Jarman, “Frisch, Fromm, Fröhlich, Frei”, Musicologica Austriaca (2017), https://www.musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/pdf/34 : the row and its inversion are on the solo violin in bars 15–27.

cues.title: Portrait of Manon Gropius
cues.text: Michael Steinberg describes the two movements as a portrait of Manon Gropius and a drama of “death and transfiguration”. Berg thought of the Andante as a Praeludium.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the two movements “represent respectively a portrait of Manon Gropius and a drama of ‘death and transfiguration’”; the Andante, “which Berg thought of as a Praeludium”.

cues.title: Allegretto
cues.text: The Allegretto follows the Andante. Berg marks the violin’s sweet thirds “wienerisch” (Viennese) and a rougher passage “rustico”, and the hiccup of a yodel is heard.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the Andante “soon leads to” the Allegretto, with the sweet thirds in the violin to be played “wienerisch”, a more bumpkin-like passage “rustico”, and “the hiccup of the yodel”.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Review of the set, 1941
cues.text: The American Music Lover reviewed the set in September 1941. It wrote that “musicianship and taste are strikingly displayed in this performance” and praised Rodzinski’s “clarity of line and detail”.
cues.evidence: The American Music Lover (later The American Record Guide), vol. 8 no. 1, September 1941, review of Columbia set M-465, pp. 17–18, https://archive.org/details/sim_american-record-guide_1941-09_8_1: review signed P. H. R. of Columbia set M-465.

cues.title: The Carinthian folk song
cues.text: Ernst Krenek identified the Carinthian folk song in 1957. Bryan Simms and Charlotte Erwin give its title as “A Vögele af’n Zweschpm-bam” and call it a yodelling song with a saucy, ribald text. In this movement it is passed among horn, solo violin and two trumpets.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, “Violin Concerto (Berg)”: Krenek’s identification in 1957 and the description by Simms and Erwin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Berg) . Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the folk song is passed among horn, solo violin and two trumpets.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Berg died in 1935, so the work has been in the public domain in the EU and other life-plus-70 countries since 2006; IMSLP also marks it public domain in Canada and in life-plus-50 countries. IMSLP considers it probably still protected in the United States.
fields.note: Rights in the composition are stated separately from rights in the recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first published before 1963; reviewed in September 1941 and listed in Columbia’s catalogue of 1942.
fields.note: The Internet Archive item carries a CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 licence label from the uploader. That label does not meet the site’s licence rules and is not relied on. The United States status of a 1940 recording is not established.

composer.epithet: Composer of Wozzeck, an opera about an exploited soldier, and of a twelve-note concerto that quotes a Bach chorale and is dedicated to the memory of Manon Gropius.
facts: Vienna; a summer house by the Wörthersee from 1932
Violin Concerto, 1935; commissioned by Louis Krasner, dedicated to Manon Gropius
composer.background:
In 1904 Berg’s brother Charly secretly took some of Alban’s songs to Arnold Schoenberg. Their sister Smaragda had spotted an advertisement for lessons in harmony and counterpoint. Alban was nineteen, a bookseller’s son from Vienna, writing songs and working in the civil service. His father had died four years earlier, and there was little money for tuition. Schoenberg accepted him all the same, though he could not pay the fee. Recalling their first meeting in a recording made in 1949, Schoenberg described “a very tall youngster and extremely timid”, whose songs stood stylistically between Hugo Wolf and Brahms.

An inheritance in 1906 allowed Berg to leave the office. When his mother proposed the conservatoire, Schoenberg heard, he wept until she agreed he could stay with his teacher. Lessons lasted until 1910. The Piano Sonata, Op. 1, completed in 1908, shows Schoenberg’s developing variation at work: small phrases change and grow, through whole-tone passages to a final B minor. The String Quartet, Op. 3, shares its themes between two movements; its opening idea returns near the close.
